claim: Myogenin is required in murine myoblasts for the localization of MTOC proteins to the nuclear envelope.
source: Here, we find that the transcription factor myogenin is required in murine myoblasts for the localization of MTOC proteins to the nuclear envelope.
evidence: Supported by siRNA depletion experiments showing that myogenin knockdown reduces PCM-1, PCNT, and AKAP9 localization to the nuclear envelope in C2C12 cells (Figure 1E-F).

claim: Myogenin is sufficient in fibroblasts for nuclear envelope MTOC (NE-MTOC) formation.
source: Moreover, myogenin is sufficient in fibroblasts for nuclear envelope MTOC (NE-MTOC) formation and centrosome attenuation.
evidence: Demonstrated by ectopic expression of myogenin in NIH3T3 fibroblasts inducing nuclear envelope localization of PCM-1, PCNT, and AKAP9 (Figure 2).

claim: Myogenin is sufficient in fibroblasts for centrosome attenuation.
source: Moreover, myogenin is sufficient in fibroblasts for nuclear envelope MTOC (NE-MTOC) formation and centrosome attenuation.
evidence: Shown by reduced PCNT and γ-tubulin levels at centrosomes in myogenin-expressing fibroblasts (Figure 3).

claim: Induction of AKAP6 expression is one central mechanism for myogenin-mediated NE-MTOC formation.
source: Bioinformatics combined with loss- and gain-of-function experiments identified induction of AKAP6 expression as one central mechanism for myogenin-mediated NE-MTOC formation.
evidence: Supported by bioinformatics analysis, ChIP experiments showing myogenin binding to Akap6β promoter, and AKAP6 depletion experiments showing loss of MTOC protein recruitment (Figures 4-5).

claim: Myogenin preferentially induces the transcription of muscle- and NE-MTOC-specific isoforms of Akap6.
source: Promoter studies indicate that myogenin preferentially induces the transcription of muscle- and NE-MTOC-specific isoforms of Akap6 and Syne1, which encodes nesprin-1α, the NE-MTOC anchor protein in muscle cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by ChIP-qPCR showing preferential binding to Akap6β promoter and luciferase assays showing higher activation of Akap6β promoter compared to Akap6α (Figure 7).

claim: Myogenin preferentially induces the transcription of muscle- and NE-MTOC-specific isoforms of Syne1.
source: Promoter studies indicate that myogenin preferentially induces the transcription of muscle- and NE-MTOC-specific isoforms of Akap6 and Syne1, which encodes nesprin-1α, the NE-MTOC anchor protein in muscle cells.
evidence: Shown by ChIP-qPCR demonstrating preferential binding to Syne1 α-isoform promoter and luciferase assays showing higher activation of Syne1 α-isoform promoter (Figure 7).

claim: Overexpression of AKAP6β and nesprin-1α was sufficient to recruit endogenous MTOC proteins to the nuclear envelope of myoblasts in the absence of myogenin.
source: Overexpression of AKAP6β and nesprin-1α was sufficient to recruit endogenous MTOC proteins to the nuclear envelope of myoblasts in the absence of myogenin.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-expression experiments in undifferentiated C2C12 myoblasts showing PCM-1 recruitment to the nuclear envelope (Figure 7G).

claim: AKAP6 is a novel NE-MTOC component in muscle cells.
source: Taken together, our results illuminate how mammals transcriptionally control the switch from a centrosomal MTOC to an NE-MTOC and identify AKAP6 as a novel NE-MTOC component in muscle cells.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence showing AKAP6 localization at the nuclear envelope in differentiated C2C12 cells and myotubes (Figure 4E-F).

claim: The centrosomal MTOC is pivotal for cell cycle progression and correct chromosome segregation during mitosis.
source: The centrosomal MTOC is pivotal for cell cycle progression and correct chromosome segregation during mitosis (Hinchcliffe et al., 2001; Khodjakov and Rieder, 2001; Sir et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MTOC function is assigned to non-centrosomal sites (ncMTOCs) during differentiation of various cell types.
source: In contrast, MTOC function is assigned to non-centrosomal sites (ncMTOCs) during differentiation of various cell types (Sanchez and Feldman, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In striated muscle cells, ncMTOCs form at the nuclear envelope.
source: In striated (i.e., heart and skeletal) muscle cells, ncMTOCs form at the nuclear envelope and contribute to correct nuclei positioning in skeletal myotubes (Elhanany-Tamir et al., 2012; Espigat-Georger et al., 2016; Gimpel et al., 2017; Kronebusch and Singer, 1987; Tassin et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NE-MTOCs contribute to correct nuclei positioning in skeletal myotubes.
source: In striated (i.e., heart and skeletal) muscle cells, ncMTOCs form at the nuclear envelope and contribute to correct nuclei positioning in skeletal myotubes (Elhanany-Tamir et al., 2012; Espigat-Georger et al., 2016; Gimpel et al., 2017; Kronebusch and Singer, 1987; Tassin et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Human myopathies, such as centronuclear myopathy (CNM) or Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy (EDMD), often feature mislocalized nuclei.
source: Notably, human myopathies, such as centronuclear myopathy (CNM) or Emery–Dreifuss muscular dystrophy (EDMD), often feature mislocalized nuclei (Jungbluth and Gautel, 2014; Madej-Pilarczyk and Kochański, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The transcription factor trachealess is required for the spastin-mediated release of centrosomal components from the centrosome in Drosophila tracheal cells.
source: It was shown that the transcription factor trachealess, which specifies tracheal fate, is required for the spastin-mediated release of centrosomal components from the centrosome and their subsequent Piopio-mediated anchoring to the apical membrane (Brodu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Myogenin acts as a unique regulator of terminal differentiation during myogenesis.
source: The MRF myogenin acts as a unique regulator of terminal differentiation during myogenesis.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about myogenin's role in muscle differentiation.

claim: In the absence of myogenin in vivo, embryonic myofiber formation is disturbed and the second wave of fetal myogenesis is largely abolished.
source: In the absence of myogenin in vivo, embryonic myofiber formation is disturbed and the second wave of fetal myogenesis is largely abolished (Hasty et al., 1993; Nabeshima et al., 1993; Venuti et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MRFs are able to induce phenotypical markers of skeletal muscle in permissive non-muscle cells.
source: Notably, MRFs are able to induce phenotypical markers of skeletal muscle in permissive non-muscle cells (Braun et al., 1990; Braun et al., 1989; Comai and Tajbakhsh, 2014; Davis et al., 1987; Edmondson and Olson, 1989; Weintraub et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NE-MTOC formation involves the localization of different MTOC proteins to the nuclear envelope, including PCNT, CDK5RAP2, AKAP9, and γ-tubulin.
source: NE-MTOC formation involves the localization of different MTOC proteins to the nuclear envelope. These include the PCM components pericentrin (PCNT), CDK5RAP2, and AKAP9 (also known as AKAP450) as well as γ-tubulin, key component of γ-tubulin ring complexes (γTuRCs) (Bugnard et al., 2005; Espigat-Georger et al., 2016; Gimpel et al., 2017; Srsen et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: At the nuclear envelope of myotubes, microtubule nucleation appears to specifically depend on AKAP9.
source: At the nuclear envelope of myotubes, microtubule nucleation appears to specifically depend on AKAP9 (Gimpel et al., 2017) and γ-tubulin (Bugnard et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: At the nuclear envelope of myotubes, microtubule nucleation appears to specifically depend on γ-tubulin.
source: At the nuclear envelope of myotubes, microtubule nucleation appears to specifically depend on AKAP9 (Gimpel et al., 2017) and γ-tubulin (Bugnard et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The localization of MTOC proteins at the nuclear envelope depends on the muscle-specific α-isoform of the outer nuclear membrane protein nesprin-1.
source: The localization of MTOC proteins at thstate nuclear envelope depends on the muscle-specific α-isoform of the outer nuclear membrane protein nesprin-1 (Espigat-Georger et al., 2016; Gimpel et al., 2017; Holt, 2016; Randles et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In cardiomyocytes, AKAP6 acts as an adapter between nesprin-1α and the MTOC proteins PCNT and AKAP9.
source: Additionally, we recently discovered that – in cardiomyocytes – the large scaffold protein AKAP6 acts as an adapter between nesprin-1α and the MTOC proteins PCNT and AKAP9 (Vergarajauregui et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature from the authors' lab.

claim: 49.1% ± 7% of C2C12 nuclei were MyoD+ after 1 day of differentiation.
source: Immunofluorescence analyses of C2C12 cells 1 day after induction of differentiation revealed that 49.1% ± 7% of nuclei were MyoD+, 12% ± 0.9% were myogenin+, 7.8% ± 0.3% were nesprin-1α+, and 1.9% ± 0.3% were PCM-1+ (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: 12% ± 0.9% of C2C12 nuclei were myogenin+ after 1 day of differentiation.
source: Immunofluorescence analyses of C2C12 cells 1 day after induction of differentiation revealed that 49.1% ± 7% of nuclei were MyoD+, 12% ± 0.9% were myogenin+, 7.8% ± 0.3% were nesprin-1α+, and 1.9% ± 0.3% were PCM-1+ (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: 7.8% ± 0.3% of C2C12 nuclei were nesprin-1α+ after 1 day of differentiation.
source: Immunofluorescence analyses of C2C12 cells 1 day after induction of differentiation revealed that 49.1% ± 7% of nuclei were MyoD+, 12% ± 0.9% were myogenin+, 7.8% ± 0.3% were nesprin-1α+, and 1.9% ± 0.3% were PCM-1+ (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: 1.9% ± 0.3% of C2C12 nuclei were PCM-1+ after 1 day of differentiation.
source: Immunofluorescence analyses of C2C12 cells 1 day after induction of differentiation revealed that 49.1% ± 7% of nuclei were MyoD+, 12% ± 0.9% were myogenin+, 7.8% ± 0.3% were nesprin-1α+, and 1.9% ± 0.3% were PCM-1+ (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: Prominent MyoD expression was detected in all cells that had upregulated nesprin-1α.
source: Prominent MyoD expression was detected in all cells that had upregulated nesprin-1α and recruited PCM1 to the nuclear envelope (Figure 1A and B), suggesting that MyoD-driven early differentiation is required for both steps of NE-MTOC formation.
evidence: Observed in immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Prominent MyoD expression was detected in all cells that had recruited PCM1 to the nuclear envelope.
source: Prominent MyoD expression was detected in all cells that had upregulated nesprin-1α and recruited PCM1 to the nuclear envelope (Figure 1A and B), suggesting that MyoD-driven early differentiation is required for both steps of NE-MTOC formation.
evidence: Observed in immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Myogenin was detected in all PCM1+ nuclei.
source: In contrast, the late differentiation factor myogenin was detected in all PCM1+ nuclei (Figure 1B) but only in 42% of nesprin-1+ nuclei (Figure 1A and D).
evidence: Observed in immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Myogenin was detected in only 42% of nesprin-1+ nuclei.
source: In contrast, the late differentiation factor myogenin was detected in all PCM1+ nuclei (Figure 1B) but only in 42% of nesprin-1+ nuclei (Figure 1A and D).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 1A and D.

claim: Knockdown of myogenin reduced the number of PCM-1+ nuclei from 11.6% ± 1.3% in control siRNA-treated cells to 2.3% ± 0.8%.
source: By contrast, knockdown of myogenin reduced the number of PCM-1+ nuclei from 11.6% ± 1.3% in control siRNA-treated cells to 2.3% ± 0.8% (Figure 1E and F) whereby PCM-1 retained a centrosomal localization pattern at highly nesprin-1α+ nuclei in myogenin-depleted cultures (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), although the pattern was less focused than in undifferentiated myoblasts.
evidence: Quantified from siRNA depletion experiments shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: Myogenin knockdown reduced PCNT+ nuclei from 6.9% ± 0.1% to 1.4% ± 0.1%.
source: Similarly, PCNT+ nuclei were reduced from 6.9% ± 0.1% to 1.4% ± 0.1% and AKAP9+ nuclei showed a reduction from 6.8% ± 0.5% to 1.4% ± 0.1% (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Quantified from siRNA depletion experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Myogenin knockdown reduced AKAP9+ nuclei from 6.8% ± 0.5% to 1.4% ± 0.1%.
source: Similarly, PCNT+ nuclei were reduced from 6.9% ± 0.1% to 1.4% ± 0.1% and AKAP9+ nuclei showed a reduction from 6.8% ± 0.5% to 1.4% ± 0.1% (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Quantified from siRNA depletion experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Depletion of PCM-1 reduced the percentage of C2C12 nuclei fully or partially positive for PCNT after 2 days of differentiation from 5.8% ± 1% to 0.8% ± 0.2% and 2.7% ± 0.9% to 0.5% ± 0.1%, respectively.
source: Depletion of PCM-1 reduced the percentage of C2C12 nuclei fully or partially positive for PCNT after 2 days of differentiation from 5.8% ± 1% to 0.8% ± 0.2% and 2.7% ± 0.9% to 0.5% ± 0.1%, respectively (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: Quantified from PCM-1 depletion experiments shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: PCM-1 depletion did not affect recruitment of AKAP9.
source: In contrast, PCM-1 depletion did not affect recruitment of AKAP9 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Shown by quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Expression of MyoD-GFP induced nuclear envelope localization of PCM-1 in a subset of GFP+ NIH3T3 cells.
source: By contrast, expression of MyoD-GFP and, surprisingly, myogenin-GFP induced nuclear envelope localization of PCM-1 in a subset of GFP+ cells (Figure 2A and B), suggesting that both MRFs are sufficient individually to induce localization of MTOC proteins to the nuclear envelope.
evidence: Observed in transfection experiments shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Expression of myogenin-GFP induced nuclear envelope localization of PCM-1 in a subset of GFP+ NIH3T3 cells.
source: By contrast, expression of MyoD-GFP and, surprisingly, myogenin-GFP induced nuclear envelope localization of PCM-1 in a subset of GFP+ cells (Figure 2A and B), suggesting that both MRFs are sufficient individually to induce localization of MTOC proteins to the nuclear envelope.
evidence: Observed in transfection experiments shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Myogenin induces nuclear envelope localization of PCM-1 more efficiently than MyoD.
source: Quantification of (A) demonstrating that myogenin induces nuclear envelope localization of PCM‑1 more efficiently than MyoD.
evidence: Quantified from transfection experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: High myogenin levels were observed in MyoD-GFP-expressing cells that had recruited PCM-1 to the nuclear envelope.
source: Analyzing endogenous myogenin expression in MyoD-GFP-expressing cells, we observed high myogenin levels in cells that had recruited PCM-1 to the nuclear envelope compared to MyoD-GFP-expressing cells where PCM-1 was absent from the nuclear envelope (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Observed in immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Depletion of myogenin in NIH3T3 cells abrogated the MyoD-GFP-induced localization of PCM-1 to the nuclear envelope.
source: In addition, depletion of myogenin in NIH3T3 cells abrogated the MyoD-GFP-induced localization of PCM-1 to the nuclear envelope (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Shown by siRNA depletion experiments in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MyoD depletion reduced Myog levels in differentiating C2C12 cells.
source: While MyoD depletion also reduced Myog levels, Myod1 levels were not detectably affected in myogenin-depleted cultures.
evidence: Shown by RT-PCR analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Myod1 levels were not detectably affected in myogenin-depleted C2C12 cultures.
source: While MyoD depletion also reduced Myog levels, Myod1 levels were not detectably affected in myogenin-depleted cultures.
evidence: Shown by RT-PCR analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Dox treatment of MYOG-mScarlet cells induced nuclear envelope localization of PCM-1, PCNT, and AKAP9.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis revealed that Dox treatment induced nuclear envelope localization of PCM-1, PCNT, and AKAP9 (Figure 2C, E and G).
evidence: Observed in immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 2C, E, and G.

claim: Median PCM-1 nuclear envelope coverage increases from 12.5% in mScarlet cells to 30.3% in MYOG-mScarlet cells.
source: Quantification revealed that median PCM-1 nuclear envelope coverage increases from 12.5% in mScarlet cells to 30.3% in MYOG-mScarlet cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Median PCNT nuclear envelope coverage increases from 8.2% in mScarlet cells to 23.1% in MYOG-mScarlet cells.
source: PCNT was recruited with an increase of the median coverage from 8.2% in mScarlet cells to 23.1% in MYOG-mScarlet cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Median AKAP9 nuclear envelope coverage increases from 3.6% to 6.2% in MYOG-mScarlet cells.
source: AKAP9, which is essential for microtubule nucleation at the nuclear envelope (Gimpel et al., 2017), coverage increased only moderately from 3.6% to 6.2%, suggesting that AKAP9 recruitment is less efficient in MYOG-mScarlet cells compared to PCM-1 and PCNT (Figure 2H).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Dox treatment of MYOG-mScarlet cells resulted in nesprin-1+ nuclei.
source: Dox treatment resulted in nesprin-1+ nuclei (Figure 2I), and RT-PCR analysis confirmed that the α-isoform transcript of Syne1 is upregulated upon myogenin induction (Figure 2J).
evidence: Observed in immunofluorescence shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The α-isoform transcript of Syne1 is upregulated upon myogenin induction in MYOG-mScarlet cells.
source: Dox treatment resulted in nesprin-1+ nuclei (Figure 2I), and RT-PCR analysis confirmed that the α-isoform transcript of Syne1 is upregulated upon myogenin induction (Figure 2J).
evidence: Confirmed by RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Myogenin binds the α-isoform promoter in Syne1.
source: PCR amplification was successful from myogenin-precipitated DNA but not from IgG1 control (Figure 2K), indicating that myogenin binds the α-isoform promoter in Syne1.
evidence: Demonstrated by ChIP-PCR shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Median nuclear envelope coverage by microtubules increased from 10.1% in mScarlet cells to 18.4% in MYOG-mScarlet cells after microtubule regrowth.
source: Quantification revealed that median nuclear envelope coverage increased from 10.1% in mScarlet cells to 18.4% in MYOG-mScarlet cells.
evidence: Quantified from microtubule regrowth experiments shown in Figure 2L-M.

claim: Dox stimulation resulted in a significant reduction of PCNT levels at centrioles in MYOG-mScarlet cells when compared to Dox-treated mScarlet cells.
source: Dox stimulation resulted in a significant reduction of PCNT levels at centrioles in MYOG-mScarlet cells when compared to Dox-treated mScarlet cells (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Levels of Cep135 did not change significantly upon myogenin induction.
source: In contrast, levels of Cep135, a centriole-associated protein, which does not relocalize to the nuclear envelope in muscle cells, did not change significantly upon myogenin induction (Figure 3C and D), indicating that myogenin affects centrosomal localization of PCM proteins but not of centriole-associated proteins.
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Induced MYOG-mScarlet cells displayed a significant reduction in centrosomal γ-tubulin levels compared to mScarlet control cells.
source: Induced MYOG-mScarlet cells displayed a significant reduction in centrosomal γ-tubulin levels compared to mScarlet control cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Centrosomes still nucleated microtubules in MYOG-mScarlet cells that exhibited microtubule nucleation at the nuclear envelope.
source: Analyzing microtubule regrowth, we observed that centrosomes still nucleated microtubules in MYOG-mScarlet cells that exhibited microtubule nucleation at the nuclear envelope (Figure 3F).
evidence: Observed in microtubule regrowth experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: α-tubulin signal at centrioles was less intense in MYOG-mScarlet cells compared to mScarlet cells, indicating a reduced MTOC activity.
source: However, α-tubulin signal at centrioles was less intense in MYOG-mScarlet cells compared to mScarlet cells, indicating a reduced MTOC activity (Figure 3F).
evidence: Observed in microtubule regrowth experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The promoters of 2462 genes were bound by myogenin at 24 hr, 60 hr, and 7 days of differentiation.
source: Therefore, we considered only those myogenin-binding sites in our analysis that were detected in the ChIP-seq data set at 24 hr, 60 hr, and 7 days of differentiation. The promoters of 2462 genes were bound by myogenin at these three time points (Figure 4B).
evidence: Determined by bioinformatics analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 748 genes are potential direct myogenin target genes that are upregulated during C2C12 differentiation.
source: We then intersected these 2462 genes with a list of 3800 genes, which were upregulated in the RNA-seq data set at both 3 days and 7 days of differentiation when compared to proliferating myoblasts (Figure 4B). This intersection yielded a list of 748 potential direct myogenin target genes (Figure 4B).
evidence: Determined by bioinformatics analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 107 myogenin targets potentially mediate NE-MTOC formation based on upregulation during rat heart development.
source: This strategy helped to further reduce the number of candidate genes to 107 myogenin targets that potentially mediate NE-MTOC formation (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Determined by bioinformatics analysis integrating multiple datasets.

claim: Four genes matched the Gene Ontology cellular component search terms 'nuclear membrane' and 'nuclear envelope': Akap6, Dmpk, Rb1cc1, and Tmem38a.
source: To this end, we utilized Gene Ontology analysis to identify candidates that are annotated to localize at the nuclear envelope (Figure 4A). Four genes matched the Gene Ontology cellular component search terms 'nuclear membrane' and 'nuclear envelope': Akap6, Dmpk, Rb1cc1, and Tmem38a.
evidence: Determined by Gene Ontology analysis.

claim: Myogenin directly binds and activates the promoter of Akap6.
source: Previous studies indicated that myogenin directly binds and activates the promoter of Akap6 (Lee et al., 2015), which encodes the large scaffold A-kinase anchoring protein (AKAP) 6 (also known as mAKAP).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: AKAP6 localizes to the nuclear envelope of cardiomyocytes through interaction with the N-terminal spectrin domains of nesprin-1α.
source: AKAP6 has been described to localize to the nuclear envelope of cardiomyocytes through interaction with the N-terminal spectrin domains of nesprin-1α and to act as a signaling hub by assembling signaling proteins such as protein kinase A, ryanodine receptor, phosphodiesterase 4D3, and phospholipase C (Kapiloff et al., 1999; Pare et al., 2005; Passariello et al., 2015; Ruehr et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Proximity labeling indicated that AKAP6 is an interactor of nesprin-1α in C2C12 myotubes.
source: Furthermore, proximity labeling indicated that AKAP6 is an interactor of nesprin-1α in C2C12 myotubes (Gimpel et al., 2017) and a recent study in our lab identified AKAP6 as a key organizer of the NE-MTOC in cardiomyocytes (Vergarajauregui et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: AKAP6 is a key organizer of the NE-MTOC in cardiomyocytes.
source: Furthermore, proximity labeling indicated that AKAP6 is an interactor of nesprin-1α in C2C12 myotubes (Gimpel et al., 2017) and a recent study in our lab identified AKAP6 as a key organizer of the NE-MTOC in cardiomyocytes (Vergarajauregui et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature from the authors' lab.

claim: Myogenin binds an E-box in the Akap6β promoter region.
source: We could amplify an E-box-containing region of the β-isoform promoter after ChIP using an anti-myogenin antibody (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by ChIP-PCR shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The β-isoform of Akap6 is upregulated after Dox stimulation in MYOG-mScarlet cells.
source: Consistently, RT-PCR analysis showed that the β-isoform of Akap6 is upregulated after Dox stimulation (Figure 4D).
evidence: Shown by RT-PCR analysis in Figure 4D.

claim: All AKAP6+ nuclei were nesprin-1α+ in C2C12 cells after 2 days differentiation.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis at 2 days differentiation showed that all AKAP6+ nuclei were nesprin-1α+ (Figure 4E).
evidence: Observed in immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: AKAP6 mainly localizes at the cytoplasmic side of nesprin-1α.
source: In addition, high-resolution microscopy suggested that AKAP6 mainly localizes at the cytoplasmic side of nesprin-1α (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Observed by high-resolution microscopy shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expression of nesprin-1α and nuclear membrane localization of AKAP6 were abolished in myotubes carrying the SYNE1 mutation.
source: Whereas nesprin-1α and AKAP6 localized to the nuclear envelope of myotubes from healthy donors, expression of nesprin-1α and nuclear membrane localization of AKAP6 were abolished in myotubes carrying the SYNE1 mutation.
evidence: Observed in patient-derived myotubes shown in Figure 4G.

claim: 12.3% ± 0.6% of C2C12 nuclei were AKAP6+ after 2 days of differentiation.
source: In C2C12 cultures differentiated for 2 days, 12.3% ± 0.6% of nuclei were AKAP6+ and 10.4% ± 1.2% of nuclei were PCM-1+ (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: 10.4% ± 1.2% of C2C12 nuclei were PCM-1+ after 2 days of differentiation.
source: In C2C12 cultures differentiated for 2 days, 12.3% ± 0.6% of nuclei were AKAP6+ and 10.4% ± 1.2% of nuclei were PCM-1+ (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Quantified from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: AKAP6 was found at all nuclei that had recruited PCM-1.
source: Importantly, AKAP6 was found at all nuclei that had recruited PCM-1.
evidence: Observed in immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Transfection of differentiating C2C12 cultures with Akap6 siRNA significantly reduced the number of AKAP6+ nuclei from 12.3% ± 0.6% to 4.8% ± 0.1%.
source: Transfection of differentiating C2C12 cultures with Akap6 siRNA significantly reduced the number of AKAP6+ nuclei from 12.3% ± 0.6% to 4.8% ± 0.1% and the number of PCM-1+ nuclei from 10.4% ± 1.2% to 3.4% ± 0.3% (Figure 5B) but had no effect on nesprin-1α localization (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quantified from siRNA depletion experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Transfection of differentiating C2C12 cultures with Akap6 siRNA reduced the number of PCM-1+ nuclei from 10.4% ± 1.2% to 3.4% ± 0.3%.
source: Transfection of differentiating C2C12 cultures with Akap6 siRNA significantly reduced the number of AKAP6+ nuclei from 12.3% ± 0.6% to 4.8% ± 0.1% and the number of PCM-1+ nuclei from 10.4% ± 1.2% to 3.4% ± 0.3% (Figure 5B) but had no effect on nesprin-1α localization (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quantified from siRNA depletion experiments shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Akap6 siRNA had no effect on nesprin-1α localization.
source: Transfection of differentiating C2C12 cultures with Akap6 siRNA significantly reduced the number of AKAP6+ nuclei from 12.3% ± 0.6% to 4.8% ± 0.1% and the number of PCM-1+ nuclei from 10.4% ± 1.2% to 3.4% ± 0.3% (Figure 5B) but had no effect on nesprin-1α localization (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment of Dox-induced MYOG-mScarlet with Akap6 siRNA decreased median nuclear envelope coverage by PCM-1 from 22.6% to 9%.
source: Correspondingly, treatment of Dox-induced MYOG-mScarlet with Akap6 siRNA decreased median nuclear envelope coverage by PCM-1 and PCNT from 22.6% to 9% and 18.7% to 5.5%, respectively (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: Quantified from siRNA depletion experiments shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: Treatment of Dox-induced MYOG-mScarlet with Akap6 siRNA decreased median nuclear envelope coverage by PCNT from 18.7% to 5.5%.
source: Correspondingly, treatment of Dox-induced MYOG-mScarlet with Akap6 siRNA decreased median nuclear envelope coverage by PCM-1 and PCNT from 22.6% to 9% and 18.7% to 5.5%, respectively (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: Quantified from siRNA depletion experiments shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: PCM-1 can be co-immunoprecipitated with AKAP6 from MYOG-mScarlet lysates but not from mScarlet lysate.
source: We could co-precipitate PCM-1 from MYOG-mScarlet lysates but not from mScarlet lysate (Figure 5G).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation shown in Figure 5G.

claim: AKAP6 is required for maintaining nuclear envelope localization of PCM-1 in myotubes.
source: Depletion of AKAP6 resulted in the loss of PCM-1, AKAP9, and PCNT from the nuclear envelope in myotubes.
evidence: Shown by siRNA depletion in enriched myotubes in Figure 5H-I.

claim: AKAP6 is required for maintaining nuclear envelope localization of AKAP9 in myotubes.
source: Depletion of AKAP6 resulted in the loss of PCM-1, AKAP9, and PCNT from the nuclear envelope in myotubes.
evidence: Shown by siRNA depletion in enriched myotubes in Figure 5I.

claim: AKAP6 is required for maintaining nuclear envelope localization of PCNT in myotubes.
source: Depletion of AKAP6 resulted in the loss of PCM-1, AKAP9, and PCNT from the nuclear envelope in myotubes.
evidence: Shown by siRNA depletion in enriched myotubes in Figure 5I.

claim: AKAP6 depletion reduced the number of myotubes with aligned nuclei from 66.0% ± 7.5% to 34.7% ± 7.6%.
source: Analyzing the positioning and distribution of nuclei in enriched C2C12 myotubes 2 days after siRNA-mediated depletion of AKAP6, we found that AKAP6 depletion reduced the number of myotubes with aligned nuclei (66.0% ± 7.5% to 34.7% ± 7.6%) and increased the number of myotubes with overlapping nuclei (26.0% ± 6.5% to 58.3% ± 9.6%), compared to control myotubes (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Quantified from siRNA depletion experiments in myotubes shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: AKAP6 depletion increased the number of myotubes with overlapping nuclei from 26.0% ± 6.5% to 58.3% ± 9.6%.
source: Analyzing the positioning and distribution of nuclei in enriched C2C12 myotubes 2 days after siRNA-mediated depletion of AKAP6, we found that AKAP6 depletion reduced the number of myotubes with aligned nuclei (66.0% ± 7.5% to 34.7% ± 7.6%) and increased the number of myotubes with overlapping nuclei (26.0% ± 6.5% to 58.3% ± 9.6%), compared to control myotubes (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: Quantified from siRNA depletion experiments in myotubes shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: AKAP6 depletion abrogated microtubule nucleation at the nuclear envelope in C2C12 myotubes.
source: In AKAP6-depleted myotubes, microtubule regrowth from the nuclear envelope was abolished (Figure 6D).
evidence: Observed in microtubule regrowth assays shown in Figure 6D.

claim: AKAP6 depletion resulted in a reduction of p150glued at the nuclear envelope of C2C12 myotubes.
source: AKAP6 depletion resulted in a reduction of p150glued at the nuclear envelope of C2C12 myotubes (Figure 6E), suggesting that the reduced number of myotubes with aligned nuclei is due to impaired dynein activation.
evidence: Observed in immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The amount of template corresponding to the promoter region upstream of the Syne1 α-isoform transcript (nesprin-1α2) was 4.5-fold higher than the promoter region of the long Syne1 isoform (nesprin-1-giant).
source: We found that the amount of template corresponding to the promoter region upstream of the Syne1 α-isoform transcript (nesprin-1α2) was 4.5-fold higher than the promoter region of the long Syne1 isoform (nesprin-1-giant) (Figure 7B).
evidence: Quantified from ChIP-qPCR shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The promoter region upstream of the Akap6β transcript was threefold enriched compared to the promoter region of the Akap6α transcript.
source: Similarly, the promoter region upstream of the Akap6β transcript was threefold enriched compared to the promoter region of the Akap6α transcript (Figure 7D).
evidence: Quantified from ChIP-qPCR shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Co-transfection of myogenin with the Akap6 β-isoform promoter construct increased luciferase activity 10.9-fold.
source: Co-transfection of myogenin with the Akap6 β-isoform promoter construct increased luciferase activity 10.9-fold, while co-transfection with the Akap6 α-isoform promoter construct did not show a significant increase compared to GFP-transfected control (Figure 7E).
evidence: Measured by luciferase assay shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Co-transfection of myogenin with the Akap6 α-isoform promoter construct did not show a significant increase in luciferase activity compared to GFP-transfected control.
source: Co-transfection of myogenin with the Akap6 β-isoform promoter construct increased luciferase activity 10.9-fold, while co-transfection with the Akap6 α-isoform promoter construct did not show a significant increase compared to GFP-transfected control (Figure 7E).
evidence: Measured by luciferase assay shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Co-transfection of myogenin with the Syne1 α-promoter construct resulted in a 21.7-fold increase in luciferase activity.
source: Similarly, we observed a 21.7-fold increase in activity when myogenin was co-transfected with the Syne1 α-promoter construct but only a mild 2.7-fold increase after co-transfection with the promoter construct of the giant isoform of Syne1 (Figure 7F).
evidence: Measured by luciferase assay shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Co-transfection of myogenin with the promoter construct of the giant isoform of Syne1 resulted in a mild 2.7-fold increase in luciferase activity.
source: Similarly, we observed a 21.7-fold increase in activity when myogenin was co-transfected with the Syne1 α-promoter construct but only a mild 2.7-fold increase after co-transfection with the promoter construct of the giant isoform of Syne1 (Figure 7F).
evidence: Measured by luciferase assay shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Co-transfection of nesprin-1α-mCherry and AKAP6β-GFP was sufficient to recruit PCM-1 to the nuclear envelope in undifferentiated myoblasts.
source: In contrast, co-transfection of nesprin-1α-mCherry and AKAP6β-GFP was sufficient to recruit PCM-1 to the nuclear envelope (Figure 7G).
evidence: Observed in co-expression experiments shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Nesprin-1α-mCherry transfection alone did not result in PCM-1 localization to the nuclear envelope.
source: In nesprin-1α-mCherry-transfected cells, PCM-1 did not localize to the nuclear envelope (Figure 7G).
evidence: Observed in transfection experiments shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Myogenin is a downstream target of MyoD.
source: Considering that (1) myogenin is a downstream target of MyoD (Berkes and Tapscott, 2005) and (2) nesprin-1α is anchoring MTOC proteins at the nuclear envelope, this suggested that, during NE-MTOC formation, myogenin might be either dispensable or required for a second step downstream of nesprin-1α.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Nesprin-1α is anchoring MTOC proteins at the nuclear envelope.
source: Considering that (1) myogenin is a downstream target of MyoD (Berkes and Tapscott, 2005) and (2) nesprin-1α is anchoring MTOC proteins at the nuclear envelope, this suggested that, during NE-MTOC formation, myogenin might be either dispensable or required for a second step downstream of nesprin-1α.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: MyoD-driven early differentiation is required for nesprin-1α upregulation and PCM-1 recruitment to the nuclear envelope.
source: Prominent MyoD expression was detected in all cells that had upregulated nesprin-1α and recruited PCM1 to the nuclear envelope (Figure 1A and B), suggesting that MyoD-driven early differentiation is required for both steps of NE-MTOC formation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that all nesprin-1α+ and PCM-1+ cells express MyoD.

claim: Myogenin is required for a step downstream of nesprin-1α during NE-MTOC formation.
source: Considering that (1) myogenin is a downstream target of MyoD (Berkes and Tapscott, 2005) and (2) nesprin-1α is anchoring MTOC proteins at the nuclear envelope, this suggested that, during NE-MTOC formation, myogenin might be either dispensable or required for a second step downstream of nesprin-1α.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that myogenin is not present in all nesprin-1α+ nuclei but is present in all PCM-1+ nuclei.

claim: The sole presence of nesprin-1α at the nuclear envelope does not allow efficient recruitment of MTOC components during muscle differentiation.
source: The myogenin depletion experiments suggested that the sole presence of nesprin-1α at the nuclear envelope does not allow efficient recruitment of MTOC components during muscle differentiation (Figure 1F).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that myogenin depletion does not affect nesprin-1α expression but prevents MTOC protein recruitment.

claim: Myogenin attenuates the centrosome during muscle differentiation independently of inducing NE-MTOC formation.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that myogenin attenuates the centrosome during muscle differentiation independently of inducing NE-MTOC formation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that depletion of nesprin-1α or AKAP6 does not reactivate the centrosomal MTOC.

claim: AKAP6 acts as an adaptor between MTOC proteins and nesprin-1α.
source: These data indicate that AKAP6 is required for the localization of MTOC proteins to the nuclear envelope, in part by forming a protein complex including PCM-1.
evidence: Inferred from co-immunoprecipitation data, localization studies, and depletion experiments showing AKAP6 is required for MTOC protein recruitment and interacts with PCM-1.

claim: AKAP6 is required for proper alignment and spreading of nuclei in myotubes.
source: This indicates that AKAP6 is required for proper alignment and spreading of nuclei in myotubes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AKAP6 depletion results in misaligned and overlapping nuclei in myotubes.

claim: The reduced number of myotubes with aligned nuclei after AKAP6 depletion is due to impaired dynein activation.
source: AKAP6 depletion resulted in a reduction of p150glued at the nuclear envelope of C2C12 myotubes (Figure 6E), suggesting that the reduced number of myotubes with aligned nuclei is due to impaired dynein activation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AKAP6 depletion reduces p150glued at the nuclear envelope, which is known to regulate dynein.

claim: AKAP6 depletion impairs spreading of myonuclei by preventing microtubule growth from the nuclear envelope.
source: This suggests that AKA6 depletion impairs spreading of myonuclei by preventing microtubule growth from the nuclear envelope.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that AKAP6 depletion abolishes microtubule regrowth from the nuclear envelope.

claim: AKAP6β and nesprin-1α alone are not sufficient to generate an active NE-MTOC.
source: While co-expression of AKAP6β and nesprin-1α induced nuclear envelope recruitment of PCM-1 in undifferentiated myoblasts, microtubule regrowth in these cells was readily observed at the centrosome but not at the nuclear envelope. This indicates that AKAP6β and nesprin-1α alone are not sufficient to generate an active NE-MTOC.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that co-expression recruits MTOC proteins but does not result in microtubule nucleation from the nuclear envelope.

claim: Additional myogenin-downstream mechanisms may be needed to activate the NE-MTOC after MTOC proteins have been recruited.
source: However, it appears also possible that additional myogenin-downstream mechanisms (e.g., induction of specific microtubule nucleators) are needed to activate the NE-MTOC after MTOC proteins have been recruited.
evidence: Speculated based on the observation that AKAP6β and nesprin-1α co-expression recruits MTOC proteins but does not result in functional microtubule nucleation.

claim: NE-MTOC formation in skeletal muscle cells and cardiomyocytes is controlled by similar mechanisms.
source: Considering that skeletal muscle cells and cardiomyocytes (myogenin-negative) both express nesprin-1α and exhibit an NE-MTOC, we hypothesized that NE-MTOC formation in both cell types is controlled by similar mechanisms.
evidence: Hypothesized based on the observation that both cell types express nesprin-1α and form NE-MTOCs, used to guide bioinformatics analysis.

claim: Centrosomal and NE-MTOC can be active at the same time.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that myogenin expression – in parallel to inducing ncMTOC formation – attenuates the centrosomal MTOC and that centrosomal and NE-MTOC can be active at the same time.
evidence: Observed in microtubule regrowth experiments showing both centrosomal and nuclear envelope microtubule nucleation in MYOG-mScarlet cells.

claim: PCM-1 is the first MTOC protein localizing to the nuclear envelope during muscle differentiation.
source: Considering that PCM-1 is (1) important for recruitment of other proteins to the centrosome (Dammermann and Merdes, 2002; Prosser and Pelletier, 2020) and (2) the first MTOC protein localizing to the nuclear envelope (Srsen et al., 2009; Zebrowski et al., 2015), we aimed to assess whether the loss of PCM-1 affects the recruitment of other MTOC proteins to the nuclear envelope.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The C-terminus of nesprin-1α is inserted into the outer nuclear membrane, whereas the N-terminus extends into the cytoplasm.
source: It has been reported that the C-terminus of nesprin-1α is inserted into the outer nuclear membrane, whereas the N-terminus extends into the cytoplasm (Apel et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: AKAP6 depletion resulted in a reduced intensity of detyrosinated (i.e., stable) microtubules compared to control myotubes.
source: Yet, we observed that AKAP6 depletion resulted in a reduced intensity of detyrosinated (i.e., stable) microtubules compared to control myotubes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Observed in immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The microtubule network organization was similar in AKAP6-depleted and control myotubes 2 days post siRNA transfection.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis showed that 2 days post siRNA transfection the microtubule network organization was similar in AKAP6-depleted and control myotubes showing the typical organization of microtubules in longitudinal arrays (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Observed in immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.
